title: LTM Becomes First Global Systems Integrator to Launch Function in IBM Quantum Functions Catalog with AI-QEM - Quantum Computing Report
gist: LTM (a Larsen & Toubro Group company) published AI-QEM, a deep-learning quantum error mitigation function, in IBM's Quantum Functions Catalog, the first global systems integrator to do so. It claims to mitigate noise with zero extra QPU runtime, unlike sampling-heavy ZNE/PEC, with ~90-95% accuracy on ~100-qubit Heron r2 benchmarks.

insights.claim: LTM, a Larsen & Toubro Group company, became the first global systems integrator to publish a circuit function in the IBM Quantum Functions Catalog with its AI-QEM error mitigation software.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: IT services firms moving into quantum software signals enterprise channel formation around IBM's ecosystem.

insights.claim: AI-QEM is available to IBM Quantum Premium, Flex and On-Prem Plan users through the ltm/ai-qem interface and plugs into Qiskit Estimator workflows.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Native Qiskit integration lowers adoption friction.

insights.claim: Conventional error mitigation methods such as zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) and probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) run ensembles of modified circuits, introducing exponential sampling overheads that inflate quantum runtime costs.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Mitigation overhead is a major cost driver for near-term quantum workloads; cheaper mitigation improves utility economics.
insights.quote: introducing exponential sampling overheads that inflate quantum runtime costs

insights.claim: LTM's AI-QEM uses a Graph Convolutional Network-Transformer to predict per-Pauli correction factors from circuit structure, backend topology and qubit calibrations, rescaling noisy expectation values with zero additional QPU runtime, circuit repetitions or ancilla qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: If it holds up, shifting mitigation to classical inference could reduce QPU spend per useful result.

insights.claim: AI-QEM matches native IBM EstimatorV2 QPU times of 12 seconds for commuting and 23 seconds for non-commuting circuits on ibm_kingston.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Confirms no runtime penalty versus unmitigated execution.

insights.claim: AI-QEM achieved 95.06% accuracy on 100-qubit Clifford circuits at depth 45 and 90.29% on 96-qubit 2D Ising runs on IBM Heron r2 processors.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Benchmarks at ~100 qubits are relevant to utility-scale workloads, though Clifford circuits are classically simulable test cases.

insights.claim: Across 80- to 150-qubit validation suites, AI-QEM's GCN-Transformer recorded a mean absolute error of 0.343, outperforming random-forest mitigation baselines.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Comparative edge over simpler ML baselines, but no comparison to ZNE/PEC accuracy is given.

insights.claim: AI-QEM is currently limited to the IBM Heron processor family and is applied only when noisy expectation values have magnitude of at least 0.1, to avoid amplifying noise near zero.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Scope limits mean the method is hardware-specific and not universally applicable.
